standard.title: Data Displays and Distribution
standard.description: create different types of numerical data displays including stem-and-leaf plots using software where appropriate; describe and compare the distribution of data, commenting on the shape, centre and spread including outliers and determining the range, median, mean and mode
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can calculate range, median, mean and mode (from AC9M7ST01). Students can interpret distributions using mode and range (from AC9M6ST01).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create and interpret stem-and-leaf plots and other numerical data displays, describing and comparing distributions in terms of shape, centre, spread and outliers.

nodes.label: Creating stem-and-leaf plots
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students construct ordered stem-and-leaf plots from a data set and read values from them accurately.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct an ordered stem-and-leaf plot for a given data set of 10–15 values.
nodes.typical_width: Construct stem-and-leaf plots for larger data sets; split stem-and-leaf plots for side-by-side comparison; use software where appropriate.
wider: Construct a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot to compare two data sets and explain what it shows.
Investigate what stem width to choose for a given data set to make the display useful.

response_modes.reason: Constructing a correct ordered stem-and-leaf plot is a skill that requires procedural care (ordering leaves, choosing stems). Errors in construction undermine all subsequent interpretation.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who construct disordered or incorrect stem-and-leaf plots cannot read summary statistics from them in Node 2 — an unordered display makes median identification impossible and shape description unreliable.
success_criteria: Constructs an ordered stem-and-leaf plot with correct stems and leaves.
Orders the leaves within each stem.
Includes a key explaining what the stem and leaf represent.

nodes.label: Describing distribution shape, centre, spread and outliers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students describe the distribution of data in terms of its shape (symmetrical, skewed), centre, spread and the presence of outliers.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe a given distribution using at least three of: shape, centre, spread, outliers.
nodes.typical_width: Describe distributions from stem-and-leaf and dot plots; connect features of the display (clusters, gaps, symmetry) to appropriate summary statistics.
wider: Investigate how outliers affect the appearance of a display and which statistics are most affected.
Compare the distribution of the same variable measured in two different groups — what do the differences suggest?

response_modes.reason: Distribution description requires a vocabulary for varied shapes — symmetrical, positively skewed, negatively skewed, bimodal. Encountering multiple distinct distributions develops this vocabulary.

success_criteria: Describes the shape of a distribution using appropriate vocabulary.
Identifies the appropriate measure of centre for the distribution's shape.
Identifies outliers and comments on their effect.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Investigating how outliers affect different display types and statistics is rich for advancing students — it connects display choice to statistical decision-making in a way that goes beyond description.

nodes.label: Comparing distributions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students compare two distributions using displays and summary statistics, making statements about differences in shape, centre and spread.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two distributions by identifying at least one difference in centre, spread or shape.
nodes.typical_width: Systematically compare two distributions using multiple statistics and display features; draw conclusions about what the differences mean in context.
wider: Investigate whether a claim about two groups (e.g. 'boys are taller than girls on average') is supported by the data — use statistics and displays to evaluate.
Explore how sample size affects confidence in comparative claims.

response_modes.reason: Comparing distributions requires simultaneous application of display reading, summary statistic calculation, and contextual interpretation — the integration of the whole statistics strand at Year 7.

success_criteria: Makes at least two comparative statements about two distributions (using statistics and display features).
States conclusions in context, not just in mathematical terms.
Does not compare individual values as if they represent the distributions.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparative investigation design (e.g. testing a claim about two groups) is a rich task for advancing students — it requires coordinating display, statistics, sample reasoning and contextual interpretation simultaneously.
